utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The news has been received this morning of the death from natural causes of Sir Richard May who until very recently served as a Judge of this Tribunal. He was greatly respected as a person and a Judge. He will be missed. Is there a matter that was bringing you to your feet, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution wished to inform the Trial Chamber pursuant to its indications at the 65 ter Conference that should there be a witness for whom cross-examination may need to be deferred based on timeliness or perhaps serial disclosure of information, we should inform the Chamber. It appears today's witness may well be such a case. We have been getting from last night various documents that require some study. And should that be the case, I will inform the Trial Chamber after the direct examination. I just wanted to -- and additionally, just at the time of coming to court, another few documents. I'm sorry to take away from anything that was just said. I just wanted to make sure the Chamber was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we must proceed today despite the news we have had. We will consider the practical implications of what you say once the evidence in chief is concluded. Mr. Rodic, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence calls Dr. Radovan Svicevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to read the affirmation from the card that is given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. May I ask you to give us your full name.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I am Dr. Radoslav Svicevic, officer of the Army of Yugoslavia with the rank of colonel, retired. I have been retired since November 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if you would focus on my questions and make a brief pause before you start answering because all this has to be interpreted because we are speaking the same language. Can you tell me about your schooling attainment.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I have completed high school. Then a four-year school for medical activities, medical offices. The philosophy school of the university majoring in clinical psychology. I am also bachelor of sciences and a Ph.D.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, if you have published any academic papers, professional papers.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Several. Primarily in the area of depression and posttraumatic disorder, stress disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Have you published any books?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I authored a book called "Stress and Disease" and coauthored three books, rather chapters in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me the exact period when you served in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: From 1967 to 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in 1991, where were you serving?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I was in the main inspection service of the armed forces of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In 1991, did you receive orders for a transfer from that service?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you can consider that a transfer, but I was sent on the 27th of September 1991 to the area of Herzegovina, more specifically to a place called Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was it a temporary transfer to that new command?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because the entire staff of the main inspection service of the JNA was sent at the time to that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: To whom did you report when you arrived at Nevesinje?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I reported to General Jevrem Cokic who had established the command of the operational group including officers from the personnel of the main inspection service of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Then at the outset when you reported to the command of the 2nd Operational Group, were there any changes in the commanding personnel after General Cokic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: No. At the moment when I reported, there weren't any changes. Changes occurred later, ten days later approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: General Cokic sustained a serious injury while travelling in a helicopter, together with a commander of warship and then commander of the naval sector, Djurovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: He was replaced by whom?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, Djurovic was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And who replaced General Cokic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: He was replaced by General Ruzinovski, who had been chief of the main inspection service of the JNA for several years before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How long did General Ruzinovski occupy that post, if you remember? You don't have to be precise.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Nine to ten days, I think. Until the arrival of General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived at the 2nd Operational Group, did you receive a particular task?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: My arrival at the 2nd Operational Group was motivated by certain psychological and social problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But when you arrived at the 2nd Operational Group, were you engaged in some particular tasks that had to do with communicating with the other side?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was at the time of General Ruzinovski. During our first meeting which I believe took place in Milenija.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I think there was also a representative of the European Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of the usher, I would like to hand out one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, can you tell us if you recognised this document and who authored it.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: We can see it was signed by General Ruzinovski, but obviously I did not participate in its drafting because my last name is misspelled here. It says "Cvicevic," beginning with a C instead of an S. It is not important. It looks like an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: There is reference in this document to the fact that on the 11th of October a meeting was held in Vila Lovcenka [phoen] in Milenija with a representative of the European Community attending. Is that the meeting you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the meeting. And I remember I travelled to this meeting together with the General Ruzinovski by helicopter from Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who was designated as liaison officer on the part of the 2nd Operational Group and the 9th Naval Sector?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I was, and it is recorded in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was anyone but you designated to handle communications with the monitors and representatives of the European Community?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: There was also Bozidar Celibic, captain of warship, who discharged these duties during my absence from the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was anyone from the 9th Naval Sector designated to liaise with the European Community Monitoring Mission and with the other side?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was Sofronije Jeremic, frigate captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will no longer need this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we should like to have this document numbered as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is D89.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown Document P61, tab 40. And at the same time, I would also like P4 to be presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, you have in front of you a document tendered by the Prosecution during the testimony of Mr. Per Hvalkof from the ECMM. Could you please tell me first as liaison officer of the 2nd Operational Group, were you familiar with the names of these persons designated as members of the JNA and names of the people designated as members of the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All these names are familiar with the exception of Sulejman Hasanovic, lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You did not know anyone by that name?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: This is the first I hear of the person, and I certainly had no occasion to meet him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And how about the names of the persons from the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Even now, after so much time, I remember these names and certain contacts I've had with these people in the course of our meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In addition to almost all the names of the members of the crisis staff, there are telephone numbers indicated.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. Apart from Mr. Niksa Obuljen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And what about members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: The only telephone number indicated is for Mr. Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Which number is that? Will you please read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of the usher, I would like Prosecution Exhibit P4 to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Svicevic, this is a large document tendered during the testimony of Mr. Adrien Stringer. The Prosecution tendered this document. We will not dwell on it long. I will only ask you about something on the first page. If you will look under the heading "11th October."

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is this the same meeting referred to in the previous document signed by General Ruzinovski, a report on the meeting in the Lovcenka Vila?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: It's not the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about the contents. Does it refer to the same meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Timewise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please look at item 7 where it says "the general agreed with the following." And subitem (a), will you please read out what it says.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: "A liaison officer should be appointed holding the rank of frigate captain. Sofronije Jeremic, telephone number, 43 948. He also confirmed that Commander Sofronije shall have full authority to act on his behalf and to make decisions at my meetings with liaison officers."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, I shall not be needing these documents any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The substance of this subitem (a), does it correspond to what actually happened at the meeting and the decisions made by General Ruzinovski?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I believe it does. Moreover, I could add that after this meeting, a press conference was held. I believe it was in a place called Cilipi. The press conference was also attended by representatives of the foreign media.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, during the period between October and December as a liaison officer, did you participate in the negotiations with the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik and the Monitoring Mission of the European Community?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I participated at several meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were these meetings regular?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: They were supposed to take place twice a week. But sometimes for some technical problems, those meetings would be rescheduled or deferred. However, on average they did take place twice a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During those meetings, were there any talks about the way -- how to deal with the issue of Dubrovnik, how to normalise life in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: All of these meetings were about that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you receive instructions from anybody as to how to participate in such negotiations and talks?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I would send information to the General Staff and I would receive instructions from them. But that was only when some strategic concepts about the future talks would be discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown D52, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you remember some of the proposals that the JNA sent to the other side as to how to normalise life in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I have in front of me a document which is well known to me. To a large extent, I was the author of this document. However, the final draft of this document was made once we agreed with General Strugar on what our position would be. And not only General Strugar, but also all the other competent officers in the General Staff. In this case, I'm referring particularly to General Simonovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Since you participated in these negotiations, what were the reactions of the other side to the proposals put forward in this document? Or was any of the proposals objected to during the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: This document and a number of subsequent documents resulted from the meetings with the representatives of the city of Dubrovnik who -- which as a rule would take place in the presence of the representatives of the European Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you have good cooperation or what was the cooperation like during all these talks and negotiations with the crisis staff, with the European monitors?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: It was very constructive, very good. Our meetings would take place very often. There was even a degree of friendship.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, during the negotiations, were there any unpleasant situations?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: In my view, there were two unpleasant situations. The first one I remember was my emotional reaction after the death of one of our soldiers. And that was despite the fact that, before that, a cease-fire had been agreed on. This emotional reaction was the result of the fact that I saw the body of this young man who was barely 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know how he died?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: He was hit by a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And this was during the cease-fire, if I'm not mistaken?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were there regular incidents of that kind?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Incidents of that kind happened very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were there any consequences?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Most often, the consequence would be the death of our men, and those were mostly shot by snipers. This may be an opportunity for me to say that I was shot at twice -- actually, my vehicle was shot at twice as I was travelling for negotiations from Trebinje to Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown P61, tab 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, during the negotiations in October, November, and December, did you also participate in the negotiations relative to some of the places in the Dubrovnik region? And if you did, what places were those?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question. What do you mean when you say "places"?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you participate in the negotiations with regard to Cavtat or any other place in the region?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Cavtat was discussed in an indirect way. However, my active participation was relative to Mokosica. I led those negotiations in the presence of Mr. Bernard Kouchner.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the document that is before you. This is also a Prosecution exhibit that was introduced through Mr. Hvalkof. This is a letter sent to Mr. Kouchner. Can you please read the first paragraph in which your name is mentioned by the head of mission, Houten, and can you explain what this is about and whether this is correct.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I'm surprised and appalled by this. Luckily enough, I believe I have arguments that I could use against this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It says here that you personally threatened that you would kill some of the monitors and that you were so convincing that after that, some of the monitors decided to leave Cavtat. Is that correct, Mr. Svicevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I have never threatened anybody in my whole life. I have never inflicted an injury on anybody. When I went to the negotiations, I didn't carry a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you maybe aware of the reason or can you assume at least why this was indicated here?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. This is a dishonest claim which I need to dispel in another way. This is a slander, the biggest slander I've ever seen in my whole life. This was written on the 20th of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You're right there.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: However, I have proof that on the 17th, 18th, and 19th, I had very intense contacts with the European Community in the presence of Mr. Kouchner.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If you look at the first sentence, it says here that "on the 19th November 1991, you informed me that you had negotiated an agreement involving monitors in Dubrovnik." Did you participate in these negotiations and in drafting the agreement?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: The dates that I have mentioned, the 17th and the 18th and the 19th are the dates when we talked in the presence of Mr. Kouchner, and the subject of our conversation and talks was how to regulate peace in the area of Dubrovnik and how to enter Mokosica in order to show an example of cooperation that would serve for our future negotiations involving the general area and the town of Dubrovnik itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. We won't need this document any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please ask the usher to show the witness a new document. Your Honour, this is a new document, one of those that were discussed by our learned friend, Somers. This document was originally in French. It took some time for the translation to be made, and we tried to deliver it to the OTP as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Defence counsel, please. Microphone for the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, can you please look at the first page of the document which is in French.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you see your signature anywhere here?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is there a signature of Mr. Kouchner here as well?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the left corner on the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you also see the signature of Mr. Niksa Obuljen from the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. This was signed as a joint document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Are there two other signatures belonging to the European monitors who participated in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was a group consisting of several people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the third page of the document bearing the names and signatures and the date. Can you please tell us what the date is and whose signatures you can see on this page.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: The date is 19 November 1991, and the signatures refer to the map that was agreed. And I'm sure that this map with the points on it was drafted by the representatives of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So the signatures that you saw on the first page, amongst them your signature, Mr. Kouchner's signature, and Mr. Obuljen's signature, is actually the signing of the contents of the agreement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the contents of the agreement and the map that was to accompany the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And the signatures on the third page?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: They are accompanying the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, and this document --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I know that it would be called Kouchner's document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This map, does it represent the separation line between the JNA forces and the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what it was supposed to represent. The date on the map is the 15th of November. And this should have been correlated with the 19th of November. This points to the fact that we had very frequent contacts, and also this points to the fact that our talks took a long time and resulted in the passing of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And then on the 19th of November, you reached this agreement on the general protocol between the representatives of the JNA and the representative of the Municipality of Dubrovnik, and this is the title of this document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at item 2 of this general protocol, subitem B, "the retreat of the military forces of both sides further away from the previously determined lines." Does that mean that, according to this map, the positions should be adjusted on the separation line between the JNA forces and the Croatian forces? Just briefly, if you can, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: This is what it should imply. However, this was just one of the stages, and the subitem B would be important if you give me an opportunity later on to tell us something about our subsequent talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What was agreed under item C? What was agreed and what was signed?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: "The surrender of weapons to the representatives of the European Community as well as retreat under the neutral control of the military elements from Dubrovnik." This is to a considerable extent in accordance with the 11-point document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes. Tell me, since this agreement was signed by all participants, that is to say, this protocol was signed with this kind of content, as a result of the negotiations, what about the other side, the Dubrovnik side that was represented there by Mr. Niksa Obuljen? Did they comply with subitem C from the protocol?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I think that over the following two or three days, things evolved in accordance with our agreement. As far as I can remember, we entered Mokosica on the 20th. I entered Mokosica as well as Mr. Kouchner and General Damjanovic, accompanied by TV crews, BBC and French TV crews.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in case you didn't understand, it says under subitem C that "the surrender of weapons to the representatives of the European Community as well as the retreat under the neutral control of the military elements from Dubrovnik" was agreed upon. So, please wait for me to finish my question. Please listen to my question and focus on my question when you're giving your answer. Was this ever materialised, this particular item?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: No, it was not, not at a single point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What is the reason for not carrying this through, although it was agreed upon and signed?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Since this pertained to the representatives of Dubrovnik, this item did, the reason was that their side did not comply with the agreement in this particular item.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know why that happened?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, after such agreements, there is no doubt that the Dubrovnik side informed the Croatian leadership in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Objection, Your Honour. There's no basis for this. It's speculative. We ask this avenue not be pursued and stricken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There seems no actual factual basis indicated by the witness, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in that case, I'm going to move on, and I would like to ask that this document be assigned a number as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is D90.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would now like to ask that the witness be shown P61, tab 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, while you took part in these negotiations with the representatives of the European mission and the representatives of Dubrovnik, were there any higher authorities of the Republic of Croatia present?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not attend any negotiations when someone from the higher authorities of Croatia took part in such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In these negotiations, when you negotiated with the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik, was there any mention of anything like them having to consult a higher instance?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I do not recall. That was probably part of their internal way of working.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this document that is in front of you. This is also an exhibit introduced by the Prosecution during the evidence of Mr. Per Hvalkof. And this document is being sent by the head of the European Monitoring Mission in Yugoslavia, and its subject is Dubrovnik. Could you please read the second paragraph. Could you please read it.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: "The representative of the JNA" --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: No, just read it to yourself so you know what it is about.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about this document because at this time I was absent. I think that my absence was from the 22nd until the 28th of November. That was the time when, according to plan, we left to visit with our families.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In terms of the content, this end of November, as can be seen here, does that correspond to the finalisation of some negotiations that, as we can see, did become the most intensive during the month of November?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: After coming back from Belgrade, that was on the 27th, I assume it was the 27th, I intensively took part in a new series of talks. This series of talks was attended by Mr. Demistura, and on one or two occasions Mr. Kouchner as well. Our talks were geared towards the following: That demilitarisation which was carried out in Cavtat and Mokosica be carried out throughout the territory of Dubrovnik. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, so this agreement was supposed to be carried out in the entire territory of Dubrovnik. You said that all the negotiations that you took part in were geared towards that, and we saw this document a few minutes ago, dated the 19th of November. That was the surrender of arms that was agreed upon and signed. What happened preventing that?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was on the 1st of December when we reached an agreement and when we specifically said at which points the surrender of weapons would took place of the armed forces that were in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And what happened? Did this surrender of weapons take place?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: After that, a meeting that was supposed to be held did not actually take place. Mr. Kouchner expressed his dissatisfaction because the agreement was being deviated from. I remember this because my memory was jogged by an article dated the 3rd of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what this was about.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I read newspapers that were published in Serbia and Montenegro. And in these articles, it said that there were problems in negotiations between the Dubrovnik side and the JNA side. And I certainly remember that Mr. Kouchner is mentioned. He also expressed his dissatisfaction over the fact that things were not proceeding as expected. I think that the text from those newspapers corroborating this opinion of mine can be obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What is it that was not proceeding as expected and why did Mr. Kouchner express his dissatisfaction?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: The next round of talks did not take place, although that had been agreed upon. And the next round of talks was supposed to include the concretisation of what had been agreed upon before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kouchner then express his dissatisfaction in relation to the agreement that was signed and that was not being carried out? Is that the reason for his dissatisfaction?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot interpret it that way. Only that he is dissatisfied with the development of the overall situation which until then followed a constructive course and which advanced and which followed a basic logic that was there previously, that the problems related to Dubrovnik be resolved at local level until a final solution is reached in terms of the relationship between the JNA, that is to say, the federal units of the Yugoslavia that existed until then.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please look at the last sentence in the second paragraph of this document. In the second paragraph, the last sentence from the top, the second paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the one that starts with "during the meeting"?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: No. "The JNA representative." Please look at the last sentence of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: What I see is something that I can just say that is written there. I cannot really make any comments on this. It just fits into what I have been saying so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, precisely; that's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. It's unclear what is being referred to. If it could at least be read out, it would help us follow about what the dialogue is -- he is going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We haven't focussed yet on an agreed part of the document that is the subject of the comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the second paragraph of this document, it says that "the JNA representative General Raseta wanted to regard Dubrovnik as a separate issue to have negotiations conducted." And in the last sentence of the paragraph, it says: "The Croat government had issued strict instructions to the local authorities of Dubrovnik not to surrender their weapons." The document bears the date of the 24th of November. Its author is the head of the monitoring mission of the European Community in the former Yugoslavia, and on the 19th of November, together with Mr. Kouchner and the Dubrovnik side, you signed inter alia an item of the agreement that pertains to demilitarisation, the surrender of weapons. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If the people of Dubrovnik signed that agreement and if they did not hand over their weapons, is that the result of the fact that they were not allowed to do so by a higher instance?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At that time, there's no evidence that this witness would have known why anything would have been done or not done by the people of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I agree, Ms. Somers. You'll have to get the witness's knowledge more apparent before you get him to make any observation on the reason for certain things not happening, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. Since time is precious, I'm going to move on to other questions. So we no longer need this document. I would just like to ask whether we will be working in accordance with our old schedule. Should we take the break now as we usually do, or shall we take it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was thinking approximately a quarter to would be a convenient time for the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, in relation to behaviour of the other side and action taken by the other side, that is to say, the Croatian armed forces and paramilitary units, as a member of the command of the 2nd Operational Group, did you receive any intelligence concerning enemy action, movements, and the like?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you attend briefings in the headquarters of the command of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you hear on that occasion from the person in charge of intelligence what the results were of the work carried out in that field, that is to say, intelligence?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to distribute the next document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, can you tell us what this document is. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: It's one of the usual documents that would come from the command of the naval sector to the command of the operations group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It's an intelligence report, as we can see, sent to the command of the 2nd Operational Group dated 5th December.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Signed by whom?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Frigate Captain Sofronije Jeremic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was that the same man who at the same time was liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please look at item B, the last paragraph of the document, and read it.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: What catches my attention is the phrase that says "they're not for the demilitarisation of Dubrovnik." It's a departure from our strategy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it also a departure from the agreement on demilitarisation that we've just discussed?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please look again in this paragraph B. "In the conflict, in the clashes in Dubrovnik, a member of the guards was killed in the area north of Ston." Do you know what this is about?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: This is consistent with the reports made at briefings of the 2nd Operational Group by persons in charge of this kind of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of December, did you have any knowledge gained from the briefings about these clashes in Dubrovnik? Did you hear about it, noted it down somewhere?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I attended the regular meeting in the command of the operational group, the daily meeting that usually took place around 6.00 p.m., before dinner. And I remember that I also noted down in my notebook something to this effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would be grateful if we could get an identification number for this document as well as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D91.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In December, in the first days of December, did any negotiations go on with the Croatian side? Did you take part in them, or were you informed about them?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: The last round of negotiations with the Croatian side I had on the 1st of December. And after that, the Croats started to avoid meetings that had to discuss arrangements for the surrender of weapons, and that was apparently the reason why they avoided the meetings. I did not meet with the negotiators from Dubrovnik or the European Community any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did someone else replace you as negotiator with the Dubrovnik side?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I have information that Admiral Jokic negotiated on the 5th of December in Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know on whose instructions he was doing that?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that, but I know the Croatian delegation was of a very high level.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know who these representatives were?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: If you would give me some names, I would remember them. I believe one of them was called Rudolf.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was the 2nd Operations Group involved in their negotiations conducted by Admiral Jokic with the Croatian ministers? Was any representative of the group there?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Not that I know. If anybody had gone there, it would have been probably me. An important detail is that this meeting was attended by General Damjanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So the members of the 2nd Operations Group were excluded from these negotiations? In fact, they did not take --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That is not the testimony. And also, if it's explored as to who General Damjanovic is, that would be incorrect should that have been the suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we will break at this point, Mr. Rodic. And you can collect your thoughts as to how to approach the issue if you want to take it further after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we proceed, may I just raise one point to the Chamber. I apologise for perhaps being not quite as quick on the uptake, but on D91, the Prosecution respectfully requests the Chamber to reconsider its position on admission in that I believe there is a 90 (H) violation. This was not put to any of the 9th -- any -- it was not put to Admiral Jokic, which we think would have been the appropriate person to have put it to. And so far, no other officers who may have been in the -- specifically at that particular location which this witness was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I really don't know how far most of the contents of 91 would gain anything from being put to the Prosecution witnesses. And if you're concentrating on the last sentence of D91, it remains without any particular substance at the present time. I think the document will remain as an exhibit. It will be weighed for its substance and weight in due course. Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I should now only like to clarify an error from the end of the previous session. On page 24, line 19, there was a misinterpretation. So the record shows that an important detail was that the meeting was attended by General Damjanovic. I don't think this is a correct interpretation, because from what I heard, the witness did not say it this way, and I can ask the question again regarding that meeting in Cavtat on the 5th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, to correct the record if necessary, I should like to ask you if anyone from the 2nd Operational Group participated on the 5th of December in the negotiations with the Croatian side with the ministers that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, pardon me, but is the question 2nd Operational Group or 2nd Operational Group command?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question was 2nd Operational Group, and the answer was no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will follow the instructions of my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And ask you if anyone from the command of the 2nd Operational Group was involved in those negotiations on the 5th of December.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody was involved, and to emphasise that fact I mentioned General Damjanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you clarify why you mentioned him.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I believe I said that because the meeting was at a very high level, if I did not attend the meeting, at least General Damjanovic should have gone. But to the best of my knowledge, he did not go, nor did anyone else from the 2nd Operational Group go to the meeting of the 5th of December with the Croatian side, with the representatives of the Croatian authorities in Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were you at the command post of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you see Admiral Jokic on that day?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. But I can say with a high degree of certainty that I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like the witness shown the Prosecution Exhibit P104.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And before that, may I ask you, Mr. Svicevic, during your stay there in autumn 1991, during your tenure in the 2nd Operational Group, did you have occasion to read or familiarise yourself with the protests addressed by the Croatian side, or maybe the monitors of the European Commission to the 2nd Operational Group or the 9th Naval Sector regarding certain incidents or events on the terrain -- on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did it happen that you on behalf of the 2nd Operational Group addressed certain protests to the other side?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what kind of protests, regarding what?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Most often, it concerned violations of the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On whose part?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: On the part of Croatia involving casualties on our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In your negotiations with the Dubrovnik side and the ECMM, primarily the monitors, did you demand as the JNA negotiator that the monitoring mission also have representatives on the JNA side?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did so from our very first meetings. But it never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know why it didn't happen despite the fact that you constantly demanded it?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I could only offer an interpretation that I believe would not serve any purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Would you please look at this document. Are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the substance?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember I wrote it myself, and I now notice the corrections written in hand. This is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you drafted this document for your commander, General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is this a reply to the protests addressed by the monitoring mission to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: It could be, but this reflects our analysis of the preceding talks as indicated in the subject. And it is also an overview of the period from the 28th of October until the 3rd of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at this document dated 4th November 1991 addressed to Admiral Stane Brovet personally.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if Admiral Stane Brovet asked a reply from the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that he did so in his direct contact with General Strugar after which General Strugar instructed me to draft this document. But more generally speaking, this is an illustration of our cooperation with the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown also the Defence Exhibit D50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you going to identify that document for the record? The witness has just spoken about the document. There's no reference in the record to what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the document which is now before the witness is Prosecution Exhibit P104.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, will you please look at this document. Will you look at the document in front of you. The document now before you is Defence Exhibit D50. And it is a wire sent by Admiral Stane Brovet to Admiral Jokic and General Strugar. Will you please look at the new document shown to you.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that Admiral Stane Brovet is asking for a report concerning the protest made by the European mission?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe it is consistent with the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that you acted then upon your commander's instructions and prepared this document signed by General Strugar? Will you please look at item 7 on page 2 where it says that in the course of talks on the 4th of November with the representatives of the European Community and the city of Dubrovnik, a message was received at 1210 hours that fire was -- had been opened from the Old Town of Dubrovnik, which was represented to the representatives of the European mission, and it was also pointed out that the Croatian side was trying to provoke the JNA at all costs in order to discredit it. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who attended these talks on the 4th of November when this piece of information arrived?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I know that there was somebody from the European Community. I know that for sure. These talks held -- were held in the Supetar Hotel in Cavtat, and Warship Captain Zec also arrived for the talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you lodge such protests to the crisis staff of Dubrovnik and the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just about the interpretation, it's page 30, line 10. It says that Warship Captain Zec also arrived for the talks, whereas the witness actually said that it was Warship Captain Zec who sent the message, not came to attend the meeting. This is what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, did you ever receive an answer or report from the other side, from the Dubrovnik side or from the monitoring mission to any of the protests that you lodged?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, at the subsequent meetings, this was dealt with. The problems that were raised at the previous meetings were dealt with at the subsequent meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: However, if you lodge a protest and if you say that a fire is being opened from the old city of Dubrovnik at the JNA positions, did you ever receive a response from the other side with regard to any such protests of yours?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: This was an example showing that the protest was lodged in a realistic time or in realtime, in the time when our talks were being held. We received this message and immediately lodged a protest. And according to the rules, the other side promised to investigate and inform us at the following meeting as to what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you only on that occasion or on several occasions find yourself in a position to lodge a protest with regard to the activities against you from the old city of Dubrovnik during the months of October, November, and December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There's no evidence of multiple activities from the old city. There is a reference to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Quite right, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, the old city of Dubrovnik, was it in this case only that the old city of Dubrovnik and the activities from the old city of Dubrovnik are against the positions of the JNA, that it was the subject of your protest?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. There's no period of time referred to in the question. It is simply -- it's one that any answer would be really speculative. Let's get a time frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we'll leave it to Mr. Petrovic to pursue the matter -- Mr. Rodic, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question, and I'll give it the time frame. I'm talking about the period of October, November, and December 1991. According to your knowledge, during that period of time, was this the only protest lodged by the JNA on the occasion of fire being opened from the old city of Dubrovnik on the JNA positions?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: There were several such protests.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at the last paragraph, there's a reference here to the representative of the mission, Mr. Lucas. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did anything come into your conversation with Mr. Lucas with regard to the detained member of the JNA member in Dubrovnik? Was that issue discussed with Mr. Lucas?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Is there any need for me to interpret?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'll kindly ask you to speed up a little.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In our conversation with the representative of the city of Dubrovnik, we received information that three of our officers had been captured. We wanted to find out their names. We insisted on their being revealed to us. However, at a subsequent meeting, they gave us only two names. At the next meeting, they didn't give us the name of the third officer, and we were afraid that this person might no longer be alive. And we requested information about that from the representatives of the European monitoring mission. Mr. Lucas denied that this third officer had died. According to him, only one dog had been killed in Dubrovnik by that time. And we objected to that. We lodged our protest about the work of the European monitors. As a result of that, this group of monitors was replaced by a new group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: We will no longer need this document. I would now like to ask you to explain, as you were the liaison officer of the 2nd Operations Group with the seat in Trebinje, did you travel from Trebinje to all those meetings and negotiations, and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I went from Trebinje to Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you go anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to Mokosica and Kupari.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And tell us, please, when we were talking about the protests that you lodged on behalf of the 2nd Operations Group or protests lodged by the European monitoring mission against the JNA, how did you convey this information? How was this information transmitted?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: It went to the naval military sector, which means that the crisis staff from Dubrovnik, if they had a message for the 2nd Operations Group, they would deliver it to the naval military sector. And vice versa, if we had information to convey to them, we would use the same means of communication. The message would go from Trebinje to the naval military sector, and then on to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And this applied also in vice versa situation?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you have direct communication with members of the monitoring mission or the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: No, although this issue was considered. We did want to establish a direct communication line. Why this wasn't done, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, where were you on the 6th December 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: In Trebinje, in the operations group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any of the activities that you might have had on that day?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to my usual activities, I also remember a visit by a group of the European Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who visited? Who were the representatives of the European Community that paid you a visit?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Colm Doyle and another representative of the European Community, and a lieutenant colonel, a liaison officer from the command of the Sarajevo army district.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown the Prosecution Exhibit P47.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If I understand you well, together with the team of the European monitoring mission, there was an officer, a liaison officer, of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know which command he belonged to, this lieutenant colonel?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I said that he belonged to the Sarajevo army district. He was a liaison officer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at this document. This is a copy of the photograph which has been admitted as a Prosecution exhibit, and this was done through Witness Colm Doyle who testified before this Trial Chamber. Do you recognise anybody in this photo?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: General Strugar in the middle. I am not in the position to tell you which of the two monitors in the photo is Colm Doyle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And when you see the background, would this be a place where you found yourself at any point in time? Are you familiar with the background?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the inscription in the photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the inscription. I'm talking about the photo, the background. What is behind the persons in the photo? Are you familiar with the background? Can you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the command of the 2nd Operations Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will no longer need this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, could you identify for the record what exhibit that was, please. Is that P47?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is P47. And I've already said that this was a photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, did you attend this meeting on the 6th of December, the meeting with the representatives of the monitoring mission?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me who the other people present at the meeting were.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: General Strugar, two representatives of the European Community, the aforementioned officer from the Sarajevo army district who was a lieutenant colonel, and myself. There might have been somebody else, but I don't remember. I am absolutely sure about the persons that I've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who the interpreter was, who interpreted the talks?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: The liaison officer from the Sarajevo army district.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you speak English?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is that one of the reasons for which you were appointed a liaison officer in the 2nd Operations Group?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe. But that was not the major reason because all the talks were official, and there was always an official interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you make any notes during that meeting and the conversation with the monitors of the European Community?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Where did you make those notes?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: In one of my notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the usher please distribute the following documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, we have a photocopy of a notebook, and the pages are 126 to 138. Would this correspond to your notebook and the pages with the notes of that period?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you in your own handwriting make a copy in the Cyrillic script, and is that a copy of the contents of your notebook from the pages 126 to 138?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why did you make a copy?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Because the original was not very neat. It was rather illegible in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Since this is your handwriting in the notebook, when you copied this notebook, did you copy word for word what you found in your notebook on pages 126 to 138?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I copied everything word to word.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true that page 126 starts with the date, 5th December? It is not very legible on this copy.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: However, in your handwritten copy, we can see it better. Can you please tell us what the entry under this date, 5th of December, refers to.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: This -- these are notes from the meeting of the 2nd Operations Group in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... I don't see any date anywhere on any of these copies. Perhaps I'm missing something. Maybe I can be directed to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my learned friend would take a better look, the first page is the notebook, and the second page bears the number 126 in the left upper corner. And in the right upper corner, there is a handwritten date, 5th December 1991. I'm referring you to the right upper hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is not reflected in the notes that were allegedly copied verbatim.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the second page of the copy has the number 126 printed on it from the notebook. And then to the right of that printed number, in handwriting, the date of the 5th of December can be seen, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, as for the entry on page 126 that pertains to the 5th of December, can you tell us what this is about. You said that you had gone for a briefing. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: What it says here in Vojnovic -- is in Vojnovic, in part of Dubrovnik. Dual, HOS, the Croatian armed forces; and ZNG, the National Guards Corps. There were dead. There were casualties. The next word is rather illegible. And then further on, it says "about 150 members of the HOS," and then there is a sign of my own, about 2500, saying that this meant that there were about 2500 members of armed forces in Dubrovnik at the time. And further on down, "concrete cut in cubes." And I cannot recognise the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although I have the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- there is no translation of what I see of what the witness is testifying to, unless perhaps the Chamber has a different version of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As far as I can see, the translation starts at page 129.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. That's what I noticed just now, that probably when the document was photocopied and put together, the translation of the page pertaining to the 5th of December was omitted. But we're going to provide a copy of that after the next break. We are going to give you the entire document. May I move on to the second part now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Mr. Rodic, but the witness doesn't seem to take in that page 126. It's the rewrite and the translation that seem to be from page 129.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, that's right, Your Honour, that's exactly the page that is missing. That is to say, of the rewrite and of the translation. This document is not complete, therefore, and we are going to take care of it already during the following break, and I do apologise for that mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we'll receive that after the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, when you look at this document of yours now, when you look at page 129, can you read your own handwriting here? It's more legible here. That is to say, from page 129 until 138.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what these notes pertain to on pages 129 to 137.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: These are notes pertaining to some characteristic moments of this meeting between the representatives of the European mission and General Strugar. So that in the report sent to the General Staff, the basic content of this meeting can be referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, before this meeting started, as regards the activities of the units of the 2nd Operational Group, did anything unusual happen on that day?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Before the meeting, the one that we're talking about now and that you attended and where you took notes, did you have any information to the effect that perhaps on that day there was some fighting?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, specifically did you have any information that there was any fighting taking place around Dubrovnik or at positions that were in the proximity of the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Except for a telegram that arrived --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I'm asking you about before the meeting.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Before this meeting, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During this meeting between General Strugar and yourself --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, I have to object. The witness was cut off with times about subsequent telexes. There's never been an identification of the time of this meeting. That might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have to confess that it's not very clear to me yet, Mr. Rodic, at what time the meeting occurred. I assume it was at the headquarters of the command, but that hasn't been made clear. So there's a lot yet that's unknown. And if you could be careful to get it from the witness rather than you give the answer, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I may be wrong, but I thought that I had just put a question in relation to this second part of the notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, were you at the headquarters of the 2nd Operational Group in Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, did you attend a meeting at the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A meeting between General Strugar and the representatives of the European Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who these representatives of the European Community are to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: In my notebook on page 129, it says Colm Doyle, and in parentheses it says "head of team for BiH and Mr. Sodan, operations officer."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: As for -- did anybody else come to that meeting in addition to the members of the monitoring mission?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Jovanovic, I already said so, the liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was this meeting held at the headquarters of the 2nd Operational Group in Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I think I've already answered that when I identified the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These notes on page 129 through page 138 from your diary, or rather, your notebook, do they pertain to what was said during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the content of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: I have my own notes in the notebook, and that reminds me of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was that the first time that Mr. Doyle came to the headquarters of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you make any entries in your notebook in respect of what the participants in the meeting said?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Although those are not shorthand notes of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I asked you previously, before the meeting with the gentlemen from the monitoring mission, did you have any personal knowledge of any fighting taking place on that day between the members of the JNA and the Croatian forces near the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On that day, that is to say, before the meeting, did you hear anything like that from anybody at the headquarters of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Until the meeting, until the meeting was held on the 6th of December with the gentlemen from the monitoring mission, did you have any information in terms of whether there were any casualties from the 2nd Operational Group, whether any member of the group was killed?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. There is nothing in evidence to lead to this line of questioning, and it is really testimony by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't see the point of your objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: He's leading, and discussion of casualties --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not leading. He's asking, did you have certain information?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'll withdraw my objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The answer will be yes or no, I expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, during that meeting, that is to say, bearing in mind your notes and your memory, did anybody say that on that day there was any fighting between the Croatian forces and the JNA forces?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you again. At that meeting, did anybody say that on that day, some soldiers from the 2nd Operational Group were killed or wounded from the units belonging to the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection. We are really into a testimonial, leading scenario.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. It has gone over an edge. It was close to it on one side before, and now it's really getting into detailed conversations, Mr. Rodic, so that you had better find some other way if you want to learn from the witness what he recalls or what was said at the meeting. And you can put to him specifically a direct quotation from other evidence about the meeting after you've got this witness's own recollection, if you want to get his comment on that evidence. I would also remind you that we still don't know the time of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few minutes ago I did not quite understand you, Your Honour. I thought it was a question of the date, so I kept repeating these questions pertaining to the date. But now I'm going to ask about the actual hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You said twice already that the meeting was held on the 6th of December, Mr. Svicevic. And my question is whether you know during which part of the day, what time of the day this was approximately?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: During the morning, around 11.00, say between 11.00 and 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us to the best of your recollection, and you also have these notes, what was the content of the talks between Mr. Doyle and Mr. Strugar? What was discussed there?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC
utterances.text: Since Colm Doyle was team leader for Bosnia-Herzegovina and there were corps within the operational group that were in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were discussions on preserving the peace, taking preventive measures lest there be any incidents that would infringe upon this peace.
